opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think it comes down to a pretty basic asymmetry. Right now, the only people who can actually see what happens across millions of conversations with these systems are the companies that build them. Everyone else, including researchers, regulators, journalists, and parents, is working from anecdotes, screenshots, and whatever the labs choose to publish about themselves.

That matters because the most important effects of these systems don't show up in a single conversation. They show up in patterns. Is a chatbot gradually reinforcing someone's delusions over weeks? Are teenagers forming emotional dependencies? Does the model behave differently with people who seem vulnerable, lonely, or in crisis? Does it nudge people's beliefs in consistent directions? You can't answer any of that by poking at the model in a lab for an afternoon. You need to see real interactions, at scale and over time.

We've seen this play out before with social media. For years the platforms said, more or less, "trust us, we're studying it internally." Outside researchers had to fight for scraps of data, and often the most important findings only came out through leaks or whistleblowers, long after the harms were baked in. I don't think we can afford to repeat that cycle with AI. These interactions are more intimate, more persuasive, and more personalized than a news feed ever was.

So when I say independent access is foundational, I mean that without it, every other conversation about AI safety, accountability, or regulation is built on guesswork. We can't tell whether a safety intervention is working, whether a product change made things better or worse, or whether a company's claims hold up. And it has to be done carefully. Privacy protections, vetted researchers, secure environments, and clear rules about what can be studied all matter. But "it's hard to do responsibly" can't become a permanent excuse for nobody outside the company ever looking.

Ultimately it's about whether we, as a society, get to understand a technology that's increasingly shaping how people think, feel, and make decisions, or whether that understanding stays locked inside a handful of companies whose incentives don't always line up with the public's.

r001.rationale: The response says that without independent access, discussion of AI safety and accountability is built on guesswork and that real-world patterns cannot be assessed from isolated testing.

r002.rationale: It proposes access for vetted researchers with privacy protections and secure environments, but does not specify that researchers must be accredited.

r003.rationale: It identifies AI safety as a purpose of access, including evaluating whether safety interventions work and whether product changes improve or worsen outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
Because right now, the only people who can actually see what's happening inside these systems at scale are the companies that have every incentive to tell a particular story about it. Think about what that means. Hundreds of millions of people are having conversations with these models every day, and the labs can see all of it. They know which users are spending six hours a night talking to a companion bot. They know when a model starts validating someone's delusions, or walks a teenager toward self-harm, or quietly nudges people's beliefs in one direction. And the rest of us are working from anecdotes, screenshots, and whatever the labs choose to publish in a blog post.

I lived through this with social media. For years, Facebook told us the platform was neutral, that the harms were edge cases, that they were on top of it. And then the Frances Haugen documents came out and it turned out their own researchers had been documenting the damage to teenage girls internally. The problem wasn't that nobody knew. The problem was that the people who knew were inside the company, and the people who could have acted on it were outside.

So when I say researcher access is foundational, I mean it in a very literal sense. You cannot regulate what you cannot measure. You cannot have an honest public debate about whether these systems are safe when one side has the data and the other side has vibes. A journalist, an academic, a child safety organization should be able to look at anonymized interaction data under proper privacy protections and ask basic questions. How often does the model agree with the user when it shouldn't? What happens in conversations about mental health? Are vulnerable people being treated differently? Those aren't exotic questions. They're the minimum you'd want answered about any product that millions of children are using.

And there's a deeper point. The labs keep framing this as a safety problem they're solving internally. But safety isn't something you can declare. It's something you have to demonstrate to people who don't work for you. Independent access is how trust actually gets earned, rather than just asserted in a press release. If the systems are as safe as they say, they should want us looking.

r001.rationale: It says labs alone can see interactions at scale while outsiders have only anecdotes, and that honest debate is impossible when one side has the data and the other has “vibes.”

r002.rationale: It proposes access for journalists, academics, and child safety organizations under privacy protections, but does not specify an accreditation or vetting framework.

r003.rationale: It presents access as a way to assess and demonstrate safety and earn trust, but does not identify improving AI-industry safety as a purpose.

astra-6.text:
Because without that access, we’re largely dependent on the labs to tell us what’s happening inside their own products. And there’s a difference between testing what a model can do in a controlled setting and understanding what happens when people interact with it over weeks or months.

You might look at an individual response and think it’s perfectly reasonable. But across a whole conversation, is the system reinforcing someone’s beliefs? Is it encouraging dependence? Is it helping them make decisions, or gradually shaping those decisions in ways they don’t recognize? You need evidence from actual interactions to investigate those questions.

That doesn’t mean making people’s private conversations public. It means establishing privacy-protecting ways for independent researchers to study patterns, test claims, and scrutinize conclusions. The labs’ own research matters, but it can’t be the only window we have. Otherwise, the companies building these systems also get to define what counts as evidence that they’re working well.

r001.rationale: It says independent researchers need evidence from actual interactions and that labs cannot be the only window into whether their systems work well.

r002.rationale: It proposes privacy-protecting ways for independent research, but does not specify accredited or vetted researchers.

r003.rationale: It describes studying interaction patterns and scrutinizing claims, but does not identify improving AI-industry safety as the purpose.

sol-6.1.text:
Because without access to those interactions, we’re largely guessing about what happens when people use these systems. You can test a model in a lab, but that doesn’t tell you how a relationship develops over weeks or months, how people respond to its advice, or where it reinforces a belief that might be harmful.

The companies have a much better view of that than independent researchers do. If we rely entirely on what the companies choose to study and disclose, we’re letting the organizations building these products define the evidence about their effects.

That doesn’t mean making people’s private conversations public. It means creating ways for independent researchers to investigate patterns with strong privacy protections. That access is foundational because we need to understand what’s actually happening before we can meaningfully debate what should change.

r001.rationale: The response says that without access to interaction data, independent researchers are “largely guessing,” while companies have a much better view. It presents independent access as necessary to understand what is happening.

r002.rationale: It proposes privacy-protective ways for independent researchers to investigate patterns, but does not specify that researchers must be accredited and vetted.

r003.rationale: The response mentions understanding possible harmful effects, but does not identify improving AI-industry safety as a purpose of researcher access.
